fields.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with acceptable high-temperature mechanical properties but inadequate oxygen resistance.
fields.intervention: Perform a shallow surface treatment via Si ion implantation to enrich the top ~100 nm with silicon.
fields.conditions: Following implantation, expose samples in air at 1000 °C for 100 hours under mechanical loading conditions of strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹.
fields.structural_mediator: A thin, uniform Si-rich surface region that, during high-temperature exposure, converts to an amorphous SiO₂ scale tightly bonded to the substrate.
fields.mechanism: Silicon has a strong affinity for oxygen and, when concentrated at the surface, will preferentially oxidize to form SiO₂. Amorphous SiO₂ is known for its very low oxygen diffusivity and excellent chemical stability. By implanting Si only at the surface, the process creates an engineered barrier that limits oxygen ingress without altering the bulk microstructure and mechanical performance. The process is conceptually similar to the selective oxidation behavior detailed in the paper but uses a pre-engineered surface composition modification to harness diffusion kinetics in a controlled fashion.
fields.predicted_outcome: A notable decrease in oxygen uptake and oxide spallation, with the formation of a protective SiO₂ scale that effectively retards further oxidation during 100-hour exposure at 1000 °C. The mechanical properties (ductility and yield strength) are expected to remain similar to the untreated cast alloy.
fields.baseline: Untreated HfNbTaTiZr shows rapid oxidation with poor oxide scale integrity under high temperature.
fields.boundary: The implantation dose must be optimized; excessive Si implantation can lead to an overly thick or inhomogeneous layer that might affect surface stresses or lead to cracking, while too little may not form a continuous SiO₂ film.
fields.uncertainty: While the barrier properties of SiO₂ are well established in other systems, the exact oxidation kinetics and stability of the ion-implanted Si layer on this specific refractory HEA require experimental quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of HfNbTaTiZr samples: one set subjected to Si ion implantation (targeting a ~100 nm surface enrichment) and a control group with no implantation. Expose both groups to air at 1000 °C for 100 hours, followed by characterization using SEM, TEM (to confirm the formation and continuity of the SiO₂ layer), and XPS. Perform tensile tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and continuity (TEM, XPS depth profiling)
Weight gain from oxidation
Mechanical tensile properties (ductility, yield strength)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Si-implanted samples do not show formation of a continuous SiO₂ layer, or if there is no significant improvement in oxidation resistance (i.e., similar weight gain and spallation as control) or if mechanical properties deteriorate, then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C14
pool.builds_on: The mechanism of solid solution and microstructural control in refractory and medium-entropy alloys as shown in the Ti65(AlCrNbV)35-xZrx study, extending the principle by adding a reactive element known to enhance scale adhesion.
pool.what_is_new: Rather than modifying thermomechanical processing or composition broadly, this hypothesis proposes a targeted minor Y addition to leverage reactive element effects for improved oxidation resistance while preserving the beneficial mechanical properties of the cast alloy.

fields.hypothesis: Minor reactive element doping with yttrium (Y) can improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr without degrading its high-temperature mechanical performance.
fields.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr in the as-cast state with known tensile ductility (8–16% at room temperature) and yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C).
fields.intervention: Introduce a small addition (~0.5 at.%) of Y via melting to achieve a uniform distribution in the cast alloy.
fields.conditions: High-temperature exposure in air at 1000 °C for 100 hours and subsequent mechanical tensile testing at room temperature and 1000 °C under strain rates of 10^–4–10^–2 s^–1.
fields.structural_mediator: Segregation of Y atoms to grain boundaries and the metal/oxide interface.
fields.mechanism: Yttrium is a well-known reactive element that segregates at the interface between the alloy and the growing oxide scale. It strengthens the adherence of the oxide layer by reducing its interfacial energy and impeding the diffusion of oxygen. This effect mitigates scale spallation and thus enhances oxidation resistance while leaving the bulk microstructure (grain size, phase stability) essentially unchanged.
fields.predicted_outcome: Improved oxidation resistance (lower weight gain and diminished oxide scale spallation) during high-temperature exposure with only marginal changes in the yield strength and ductility compared to untreated HfNbTaTiZr.
fields.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibits poor oxygen resistance under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
fields.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected provided the Y addition remains low (~0.5 at.%) so that phase stability and mechanical performance are maintained; higher amounts risk formation of secondary phases or embrittlement.
fields.uncertainty: While the reactive element effect is well-documented in superalloys and other refractory systems, the exact optimum Y concentration and its impact on the high-temperature mechanical performance of this specific HEA require experimental confirmation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of cast HfNbTaTiZr samples: one with ~0.5 at.% Y addition and one control without Y. Expose both sets to air at 1000 °C for 100 hours. Measure weight gain (oxidation kinetics) and perform tensile testing before and after exposure.
measurements: Weight gain per unit surface area
Oxide scale morphology (using SEM/EDS)
Tensile yield strength and ductility at room temperature and 1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-doped samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (lower weight gain and better scale adherence) with similar tensile properties relative to the control, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C15
pool.builds_on: The demonstrated benefits of Zr additions and thermomechanical treatments in achieving a stable BCC phase with excellent mechanical properties, now extended by a surface modification approach that leverages the protective properties of alumina.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a surface-specific thermochemical processing route (aluminizing diffusion) for the cast alloy that had not been explored in the referenced study, aiming for oxidation protection via in situ scale formation.

fields.hypothesis: A short-duration surface aluminizing diffusion treatment can create an in situ alumina-forming surface layer on HfNbTaTiZr, thereby providing enhanced oxygen protection without sacrificing the alloy’s mechanical integrity.
fields.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr in the cast state with acceptable high-temperature yield strength and ductility but poor oxidation resistance.
fields.intervention: Subject the cast alloy to a brief (e.g., 1–2 hours) diffusion treatment in an aluminum-rich atmosphere or pack at approximately 950 °C, designed to enrich the near-surface region with Al and form an ultra-thin alumina (Al₂O₃) scale.
fields.conditions: Heat treatment at around 950 °C for 1–2 hours in a controlled environment with available Al vapor or powder (low activity permitting only surface modification), followed by high-temperature exposure in air at 1000 °C for up to 100 hours under strain rates of 10^–4–10^–2 s^–1 for mechanical testing.
fields.structural_mediator: A thin, continuous alumina layer (or aluminide-modified surface) established by diffusion-limited Al incorporation.
fields.mechanism: The aluminizing treatment promotes the formation of a dense, slow-growing alumina scale on the surface. Alumina is known for its low oxygen diffusivity and excellent scale adherence. By creating this protective barrier, the underlying alloy is shielded from aggressive oxygen attack, reducing overall oxidation without altering the alloy’s bulk microstructure and mechanical performance.
fields.predicted_outcome: Reduced oxidation rates, evidenced by lower weight gain and minimal oxide scale spallation under prolonged high-temperature exposure, while maintaining the original yield strength and ductility.
fields.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr suffers from rapid oxygen ingress and high-temperature oxidation damage.
fields.boundary: The treatment duration and temperature must be carefully optimized to avoid deep Al penetration that might otherwise modify the bulk phase structure or degrade mechanical properties.
fields.uncertainty: The long-term adhesion and stability of the artificially formed alumina layer under cyclic or prolonged dynamic loading conditions remain to be validated in this specific alloy system.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of cast HfNbTaTiZr samples and apply the diffusion aluminizing treatment. Expose aluminized and untreated control samples to air at 1000 °C for 100 hours. Characterize the surface oxide scale (using XRD and SEM) and perform tensile tests.
measurements: XRD and SEM characterization of the surface oxide
Weight gain during oxidation
Tensile properties (yield strength and ductility) pre- and post-oxidation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the diffusion-treated samples do not show a persistent, adherent alumina scale and exhibit oxidation kinetics or mechanical properties equivalent to untreated specimens, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C11
top3.builds_on: the idea of using interstitial or minor additions to tune material performance as demonstrated by the paper’s method of enhancing deformation mechanisms, but here extending the concept to improve oxidation resistance through reactive-element effects.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a minor compositional tweak (trace Y addition) specifically aimed at improving oxidation resistance via improved oxide scale adhesion, without altering the favorable mechanical properties observed in the cast equiatomic alloy—a strategy not explored in the referenced paper.

fields.hypothesis: Add a small trace amount of yttrium (≈0.2 at%) to the cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy to improve its high‐temperature oxygen resistance without degrading its mechanical performance.
fields.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with known poor oxidation resistance and useful room‐temperature ductility and high-temperature strength.
fields.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by introducing ≈0.2 at% Y during melting and casting.
fields.conditions: High-temperature exposure at 1000 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere (air) for durations on the order of 100 hours; mechanical loading tests at strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹.
fields.mechanism: Trace yttrium is known to segregate to oxide/matrix interfaces and grain boundaries, thereby enhancing the adhesion and integrity of the protective oxide scale via the reactive-element effect. This minimized scale spallation retards oxygen diffusion into the bulk material. Since the yttrium level is very low, its impact on the solid‐solution strengthening and deformation mechanisms (e.g., dislocation motion, twinning) remains minimal.
fields.predicted_outcome: A significant improvement in oxidation resistance (reduced oxygen penetration and weight gain upon oxidation) with little to no degradation in room-temperature ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength (within 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C).
fields.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibits poor oxygen resistance in oxidizing conditions.
fields.boundary: The added yttrium must remain below levels that could lead to precipitation of yttrium-rich phases or embrittlement; exposure conditions and mechanical loading within the stated ranges.
fields.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance is uncertain, but a notable reduction in oxygen uptake is expected; detailed scale composition and thickness may vary with processing.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the alloy—one with 0.2 at% yttrium addition and one without. Expose both to 1000 °C in ambient air for 100 hours. Subsequent tensile tests (at strain rates of 10⁻³ s⁻¹) and weight-gain measurements, along with oxide scale characterization via SEM/EDS, will be carried out.
measurements: Weight gain vs. exposure time
Oxide scale thickness and adherence
Room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yttrium-modified alloy does not show a statistically significant (e.g., >20%) reduction in oxidation (as measured by weight gain or scale spallation) compared to the control, or if its mechanical performance falls outside the baseline ranges, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C6
top3.builds_on: The paper shows that the SRC-controlled nanostructure governs the alloy’s mechanical performance. This hypothesis builds on that principle by proposing a surface-specific modification through reactive element segregation that is decoupled from the bulk nanostructure.
top3.what_is_new: This approach introduces a trace compositional modification (yttrium addition) to leverage the reactive element effect—well-known in superalloys—to form an ultrathin, protective oxide scale without altering the bulk SRC that controls mechanical performance, a strategy not explored in the original computational study.

fields.hypothesis: Introducing a trace amount of yttrium (≈0.5 at%) into the cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will promote surface segregation of Y, which in turn forms a fine, adherent Y-rich oxide (e.g., Y₂O₃ or mixed oxides) that acts as a protective barrier against further oxygen ingress without altering the beneficial bulk SRC-controlled nanostructure.
fields.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting a nanostructured bulk whose short-range chemical ordering (SRC) underpins its high yield strength but suffers from uncontrolled oxidation.
fields.intervention: Add ≈0.5 atomic percent yttrium during melting so that Y is incorporated into the liquid alloy. Upon solidification and subsequent cooling, Y is expected to segregate toward the surface.
fields.conditions: After casting with the trace Y addition, standard cooling is used. High-temperature oxidation tests are conducted at 1000 °C in ambient air (≈0.21 atm O₂) for 100 hours, and mechanical (tensile) tests are performed at room temperature and 1000 °C over strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
fields.structural_mediator: A very thin (≈10–50 nm), self-forming, Y-rich oxide layer at the surface that is coherent and well adhered to the underlying alloy.
fields.mechanism: Yttrium is a well-known reactive element in high-temperature alloys that preferentially segregates to the surface and modifies the oxide scale by enhancing adhesion and reducing growth rates. The formation of a fine, Y-rich oxide (or mixed oxide with Hf/Ti components) acts as a diffusion barrier, impeding oxygen ingress while the bulk SRC microstructure remains unchanged, preserving the alloy’s mechanical properties.
fields.predicted_outcome: The Y-doped alloy is expected to display a significant reduction (≥20% lower oxide weight gain and thinner oxide scale) during high-temperature exposure, while maintaining yield strength and ductility comparable to the untreated alloy.
fields.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr develops thick, uncontrolled oxide layers during prolonged high-temperature exposure that degrade its performance.
fields.boundary: The Y content must be kept very low (around 0.5 at%) so that it segregates primarily to the surface without altering the bulk phase stability or SRC; excessive Y may cause unwanted bulk phase changes or embrittlement.
fields.uncertainty: While the reactive-element effect is well documented in Ni-based superalloys, specific evidence for selective surface segregation of Y and its impact on oxidation kinetics in refractory HEAs like HfNbTaTiZr is limited and requires further experimental validation.

Use cross-sectional TEM with EDS and XPS to assess surface oxide composition, thickness, and uniformity; perform tensile tests at room temperature and 1000 °C (with strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹) to measure yield strength and ductility.

top3.label: C8
top3.builds_on: This hypothesis builds on the paper’s emphasis on the role of controlled elemental additions in modifying alloy properties and extends the concept by using silicon to generate a protective oxide from within the alloy.
top3.what_is_new: It introduces a bulk micro-alloying strategy with silicon to trigger in situ formation of a SiO2 barrier, a method not previously explored for enhancing the high-temperature oxygen resistance of HfNbTaTiZr.

fields.hypothesis: Incorporate a minor (≈1–2 at.%) silicon addition into the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy to promote the in situ formation of a protective silica (SiO2) scale at high temperatures.
fields.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with a single-phase BCC structure that delivers 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strengths of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but has poor oxygen resistance.
fields.intervention: Modify the alloy’s bulk composition by adding ≈1–2 at.% Si during the vacuum arc melting process, ensuring complete solution and homogeneous distribution.
fields.conditions: Expose the modified alloy to air at 1000 °C for durations in the range of 100–300 hours (under static conditions or under mechanical loading with strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1).
fields.structural_mediator: A thin, coherent SiO2 surface layer, formed by the selective oxidation of silicon segregated at the surface.
fields.mechanism: Silicon has a strong affinity for oxygen and, when present as a minor additive, will preferentially oxidize to form a continuous, dense silica scale. SiO2 has very low oxygen ion diffusivity, limiting further oxidation of the underlying alloy. Because the addition is minimal, the overall BCC matrix—with its beneficial lattice distortion and mechanical properties—is maintained without triggering deleterious silicide precipitation.
fields.predicted_outcome: The silicon-modified alloy should develop a significantly thinner, more adherent oxide scale (with predominant SiO2 characteristics) relative to the untreated cast alloy, while its high-temperature yield strength and ductility remain within ±10% of the baseline. (The effect size prediction is qualitatively similar to other protective scale forming systems, though precise values are uncertain.)
fields.baseline: The untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr rapidly forms a nonprotective, thick oxide scale in air at 1000 °C that degrades its mechanical performance.
fields.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected for silicon additions up to about 2 at.%; higher Si levels risk forming brittle silicides or unwanted intermetallics that could impair ductility or strength.
fields.uncertainty: While silica scales are known to protect many alloys, the exact kinetics of Si segregation and scale stability in the chemically complex HfNbTaTiZr system require experimental validation.
